key_claims: Al-Qaeda and modern jihadism are founded on a conspiracy theory of a Zionist-Crusader alliance against Muslims.
Bin Laden was annoyed by people denying al-Qaeda's responsibility for 9/11, per captured compound files.
The Taliban's claim that the US backs ISIS is likely propaganda; some US officials acknowledged indirect support for the Taliban/al-Qaeda offensive against ISIS in eastern Afghanistan.
The theory that Assad created or controlled ISIS is rejected: the Assad regime lost territory and soldiers to ISIS, though Assad did earlier facilitate jihadists into Iraq.
US officials have 'disconnected the dots' on al-Qaeda–Taliban ties, intentionally ignoring links to fit a policy of withdrawing from Afghanistan.
ISIS was originally part of al-Qaeda before Zawahiri ejected it.
Hosts argue that analysts who 'disconnect the dots' deny the cohesive network linking al-Qaeda and ISIS to their global affiliates.
Official US designations from the Obama administration document Iran's collusion with al-Qaeda, so the claim is not a neocon fabrication.
Hosts claim the Taliban remains tied to al-Qaeda, and that Afghan press data shows many of the final 400 prisoners are dangerous, with 44 blacklisted and possible al-Qaeda links.
Hosts say the Taliban has worked to free dual-hatted al-Qaeda-Taliban figures, citing Abdul Rashid Baluch's 2019 release for three Indian engineers.
The Afghan government has surrendered to the US-Taliban deal, while the Taliban refuses to accept anything less than an Islamic Emirate and uses talks to run out the clock.
Aminullah, head of the Taliban's Peshawar Shura, is described as a dual-hatted al-Qaeda and Taliban leader running the Ganj Madrasa training camp.
Hosts argue the US could have withdrawn without legitimizing the Taliban or absolving its al-Qaeda ties.
